title: Benchmark methodology workshop - KV cache, batching, quantization (AcmeHealth)

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-12
Start: 08:23 AM PT
Duration: 1:18
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Raman (Redwood SE), Daniel Chen (CTO, AcmeHealth), Ravi Patel (ML Lead), Sophia Gomez (Infra), Maya Ortiz (Product)

[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna run a focused benchmark methodology workshop — really technical today, Priya will drive most of the runtime specifics. Quick round-robin intros?
[00:12] Daniel (AcmeHealth): Daniel here — CTO, mostly want to understand apples-to-apples comparisons and what questions we should ask vendors.
[00:18] Ravi (AcmeHealth): Ravi, ML lead. We'll provide our prompt sets and some traces. Interested in tail latency and cost tradeoffs.
[00:24] Sophia (AcmeHealth): Sophia, infra. I'm focused on VPC/on-prem constraints and KMS handling.
[00:30] Priya (Redwood SE): Great, thanks. Agenda: prompt set curation, tokenization parity, load generation, KV cache warmup and hit-rate measurement, batching config, quantization evaluation, and then VPC/on-prem notes.
[00:42] Jordan: Quick logistics: we'll aim for reproducible runs — same model binary, same tokenization, three runs to account for jitter. We'll capture p50/p90/p95/p99 and throughput.
[00:55] Ravi: Sounds good. How do you handle KV cache in your runtime? We get a lot of repeated prefixes for our chat flows.
[01:02] Priya: Short answer: we have a layer of prefix/KV caching per-worker. Important to define warmup — whether you pre-populate KV from traces or simulate steady-state traffic. For apples-to-apples you need the same warmup approach across vendors.
[01:18] Daniel: Can you quantify the impact? Like hit-rate vs latency down to ms?
[01:24] Priya: In our internal tests, a single-token prefix hit-rate change from 20% to 70% can move effective p95 by ~30-60ms depending on sequence length and batch size. But results vary by model. Also note staleness effects on cache for multi-turn.
[01:36] Ravi: Ok, so for our benchmark we should provide a representative distribution of sequence lengths and turn counts?
[01:42] Priya: Exactly. We prefer a prompt set that's stratified: short completions (<=32 tokens), medium (64-128), long (256+), and multi-turn sessions. Include their frequency so load gen can replay realistic sampling.
[01:55] Jordan: On tokenization parity — ensure you provide the exact tokenizer or tokenized inputs. Vendors sometimes use slightly different tokenizers or byte pair merges which skews token counts and cost.
[02:06] Maya (AcmeHealth): We can export tokenized corpus, we just need to understand format.
[02:10] Priya: CSV with fields: session_id, turn_index, token_count, token_ids (optional). If you share token_ids we can avoid tokenizer differences.
[02:20] Sophia: For VPC/on-prem we can't share raw content sometimes. Is token_ids enough?
[02:24] Priya: Yes, token_ids + metadata is sufficient for apples-to-apples throughput and latency tests. For quality evals you'd need text but we can do masked or hashed variants.
[02:33] Jordan: Load generation: we recommend two phases — cold-start ramp and steady-state. Cold-start ramp mimics new peak; steady-state run for 10-60 minutes to measure tail behavior under sustained load.
[02:46] Ravi: How long should steady-state be? We have variable traffic and bursts often.
[02:50] Priya: Steady-state at least 10 minutes for basic, 30-60 for production-like. If you have long-tail variability, run multiple 15-min windows. Also capture CPU/GPU utilization and memory footprints.
[03:05] Daniel: Batching — do you enable dynamic batching? What's best for low latency?
[03:10] Priya: Redwood runtime supports dynamic batching with latency SLO floors. For strict low-latency (e.g., <50ms p95) small batch sizes or even single-sample runs are needed. For throughput-cost tradeoffs we tune target batch sizes and max wait time. The benchmark should include configs: no-batching, conservative batch (max 4), aggressive (max 32) and measure cost-per-token and latency.
[03:30] Sophia: Do you measure GPU memory fragmentation or kv cache memory accounting?
[03:34] Priya: Yes — include resident GPU memory and KV cache overhead. KV cache is mostly host memory for some models; for others it sits on GPU. We'll log both. Also note model quantization changes memory amplifier.
[03:46] Ravi: Quantization — how to run apples-to-apples? If one vendor uses int8 and another uses fp16 you'll get both perf and quality differences.
[03:53] Priya: Right — best practice: define quality thresholds first. For apples-to-apples, run baseline fp16 (or bf16 where supported) then run quantized variants (int8, int8-fp16 mixed) and report both latency and quality delta on a held-out eval set. Don't hide accuracy loss behind latency gains.
[04:10] Jordan: We'll also capture token-level differences and a small set of human evals or automatic metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/semantic similarity) depending on your use-case.
[04:19] Maya: For privacy we may prefer automated semantic metrics only.
[04:22] Priya: That's fine. We'll accept embeddings-based similarity, P0/P1 label checks, or your custom metrics.
[04:29] Daniel: Regarding compilation and kernel selection — vendors sometimes tune kernels per model. How do we standardize?
[04:36] Priya: Document the exact build flags and runtime versions. For fairness, either allow vendors to use their optimized kernels and document them, or request a baseline build with conservative kernel selection. We suggest running both: unoptimized baseline and optimized vendor best-effort. Report both sets of numbers.
[04:52] Ravi: Good idea. How do you handle multi-node scaling tests? We want to know linearity as we add GPUs.
[04:58] Priya: For multi-node, define a per-node synthetic load that scales. Measure normalized throughput per GPU and look for communication overheads (all-reduce, KV synchronization). Also run single-node with higher concurrency to isolate intra-node behavior.
[05:12] Sophia: For VPC/on-prem concerns: SSO, KMS, and audit logs. We need to see integration points.
[05:18] Jordan: We'll send the security bundle: SOC2, ISO docs, SSO/SAML patterns, and KMS/HSM integration notes. For Private deployments we support customer-managed KMS and audit logs at route level.
[05:31] Priya: One gotcha: network egress and sharded KV across machines can influence latency. If you're in a private VPC, ensure that adjacency between compute and KV store is optimal or measure the extra RTT.
[05:44] Ravi: About measurement noise — how do you ensure results are reproducible?
[05:47] Priya: Three runs, controlled environment, pin CPU/GPU frequencies where possible, and capture system background noise. Use deterministic seeding for tokenization and sampling. We also attach raw p99 traces and histograms for transparency.
[06:03] Maya: Will you share the raw logs?
[06:06] Jordan: Yes, we upload the raw CSVs and the benchmark spreadsheet. We'll annotate columns: run_id, timestamp, latency_ms, token_count, batch_size, cache_hit, node_id, gpu_mem_mb, cpu_usage_pct.
[06:20] Ravi: Cache metrics — what do you log?
[06:23] Priya: cache_hit (bool), cache_latency_ms (time to fetch), kv_memory_mb, cache_evictions, and per-session cache warmup counts.
[06:34] Daniel: For our chat workload, multi-turn scenarios are critical. How to simulate realistic turn overlaps?
[06:40] Priya: Replay sessions preserving turn timing. If that's not possible, sample inter-turn intervals from your trace and inject them into the load generator. That preserves concurrency patterns and KV reuse.
[06:52] Jordan: Ok let's talk about deliverables: Redwood will produce a benchmark pack with scripts, a detailed spreadsheet, and a short write-up of methodology and assumptions.
[07:01] Priya: We'll also include recommended runtime flags: dynamic batching params, kv_cache warmup policy, quantization profiles evaluated, and the exact model binary version and compiler flags.
[07:12] Sophia: For on-prem deployment, we need a checklist for firewall rules and KMS endpoints.
[07:16] Priya: We'll add a VPC checklist and the network ports used for our runtime and telemetry. For KMS you can bring your own, and we'll show a test harness for key rotation.
[07:26] Ravi: One more — cost accounting. How do you compute cost-per-1k-tokens across runs?
[07:31] Jordan: We compute GPU time * effective utilization / tokens served, plus amortized infra costs. In the benchmark spreadsheet we'll show both raw GPU-second/token and cost using your committed pricing assumptions.
[07:44] Maya: Anything else on apples-to-apples we should be careful about?
[07:47] Priya: Watch out for hidden caching at the model-serving layer, e.g., LLM providers sometimes cache outputs for identical prompts. Make sure caching semantics are disclosed and either enabled or disabled consistently across vendors. Also verify tokenization and newline handling.
[07:59] Jordan: Great. Let's recap next steps quickly.
[08:02] Daniel: Recap would be helpful.
[08:04] Jordan: Recap: customer provides tokenized prompt set and a production trace (Ravi). Redwood runs three benchmark runs with documented configs (Jordan/Priya). Share results and spreadsheet, then schedule PoC kickoff for Dedicated behind VPC. Security docs and checklist to be shared.
[08:22] Ravi: Sounds good. We'll aim to share artifacts by Tuesday.
[08:25] Sophia: We'll review network checklist and confirm KMS requirements.
[08:28] Jordan: Thanks everyone. Priya and I will follow up with the spreadsheet and scripts.
[08:32] Priya: Thanks, bye.
